title: The 96% satisfied redesign
blurb: A glowing customer satisfaction survey with a missing audience.
prompt: Read this product launch memo written by an AI analyst. Spot the flaw in the reasoning.

segments.label: Claim 1
segments.text: Three months ago, our coffee chain rolled out a redesigned mobile ordering app.

segments.label: Claim 2
segments.text: Last week, we surveyed 1,200 customers who just renewed their annual VIP pass.

segments.label: Claim 3
segments.text: 96% of those respondents rated the new ordering experience 4 or 5 stars.

segments.label: Claim 4
segments.text: Therefore, the app redesign was an overwhelming success across our entire customer base.

segments.label: Claim 5
segments.text: No further usability fixes are needed before expanding the layout to our web store.

conclusion: Verdict: 96% satisfaction proves almost all customers love the new app.

flaws.original: Therefore, among customers who chose to renew their VIP pass, satisfaction is high — but we cannot generalize to all customers without checking churned users.
flaws.corrupted: Therefore, the app redesign was an overwhelming success across our entire customer base.

diagnosis_choices.label: Survivorship / selection bias: surveying only renewing VIPs excludes everyone who quit because they hated the new app.
1,200 people is always too small a sample to measure satisfaction.
Four-star ratings should never be grouped together with five-star ratings.
Three months is too long after a launch to collect any user feedback.

fix_choices.label: Limit the claim to renewing VIPs, and check renewal rates plus feedback from churned and casual customers.
Survey 10,000 more renewing VIPs to make the 96% estimate even tighter.
Switch from a 5-star scale to a 10-point scale for renewing members.
Average the 4-star and 5-star responses separately without checking non-renewers.

flaws.explanation: Customers who hated the redesign are the most likely to cancel instead of renewing. Polling only people who stayed guarantees a rosy score and tells you nothing about total satisfaction.
flaws.why_tempting: 1,200 responses and 96% look authoritative and statistically solid until you notice who wasn't in the room.
flaws.catch_rule: Whenever you see a glowing survey stat, ask: 'Who already left and never got asked?'
flaws.hint: Who is missing from the group surveyed in Claim 2?

practice.problem: A gym asks members who have attended 50+ times this year if the gym is welcoming, and 98% say yes. What is missing?
practice.answer: Members who felt unwelcome stopped coming long before 50 visits and were excluded from the survey.

clean_segments: Three months ago, our coffee chain rolled out a redesigned mobile ordering app.
Last week, we surveyed 1,200 customers who just renewed their annual VIP pass.
96% of those respondents rated the new ordering experience 4 or 5 stars.
This shows high satisfaction among renewing VIPs, though we must check overall renewal rates and churned users before calling the redesign a broad success.
Before rolling the layout to the web store, we should review feedback from non-renewing and first-time users.
clean_conclusion: High scores among loyal renewers are encouraging, but not proof of overall customer satisfaction.
